## Report: Reinhart & Rogoff, "Growth in a Time of Debt"

**1. The question, frozen.** The title and abstract make one thing central: *does a high public-debt-to-GDP ratio — 90% and above — go with notably lower real GDP growth, across 44 countries and about 200 years?* Kind: mostly backward ("what can we tell from what we see"), with a causal reading in the title. Range: public debt/GDP, 44 countries, ~1790–2009, growth and inflation; plus external and private debt. Held still below.

**2. The explanation in parts.** (P1) the new dataset — 44 countries, ~3,700 annual debt observations; (P2) the four debt buckets (below 30 / 30–60 / 60–90 / above 90); (P3) the 90% threshold for public debt; (P4) the size of the gap — median growth ~1% lower, mean ~4% lower; (P5) the same threshold for advanced and emerging; (P6) a lower, 60% external-debt threshold for emerging markets; (P7) no inflation–debt link for advanced countries as a group, a strong one for emerging ("fiscal dominance"); (P8) the mechanism — "debt intolerance", rising risk premia, forced fiscal tightening; (P9) the war-vs-peacetime caveat; (P10) the private-debt / deleveraging illustration.

**3. Part by part.**

| Part | Mark | Note |
|---|---|---|
| P1 dataset | **Held** | By the job "give 200 years of comparable debt numbers." This is what lets every other test run, and it is the paper's real work. |
| P2 buckets | **Fixed** | The authors say the cutoffs are "our interpretation." Owner-set, untested. A neighbour set (25/50/75/100) draws the same picture. |
| P3 the 90% line | **Loose** | Swap 90 for 85 or 100, or a smooth line with no kink: same story. What survives is only "high debt goes with worse growth." That coarser claim, worth checking, is the part actually held. |
| P4 the gap's size | **Unknown** | No test run bears on the magnitude. Settle it by re-weighting by country size and leaving out one country at a time. The paper says the 96 high-debt years lean on Belgium, Greece, Italy, Japan and post-war years. |
| P5 same for both groups | **Held if** | Held only by P3's job ("the break is at 90"), which is itself loose. |
| P6 external 60% | **Loose** | A second owner-chosen line; the Maastricht remark shows its neighbours work too. |
| P7 inflation split | **Held** | This contrast does a job: it rules out a single "more debt → more inflation" story. The US exception is a residual, unnamed. |
| P8 mechanism | **Loose** | The authors call it speculation. "Debt intolerance" is a catch-all that absorbs Australia, New Zealand and every exception — and comes with no gauge. |
| P9 war/peace caveat | **Fixed** | Stated as an assumption ("we will not attempt to discriminate"), not tested. |
| P10 private debt | **Borrowed** | Rests on the separate R&R 2009 crisis-deleveraging explanation, not tested here. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**

- **Flip.** Could the same numbers carry the opposite story? Yes, easily: slow growth → falling revenue → more debt fits the table exactly as well. The paper says "associated with," but the title reads causal, and the causal direction is never poked — nothing raises growth to see whether debt falls.
- **Direction.** As a "what can we tell" paper it is honest. It over-reaches when read as "debt causes slow growth."
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** "Debt intolerance", "risk premia", "fiscal dominance" are labels until a change tells each from a rival. The paper names none.
- **Pairs that pull.** (a) "Thresholds are country-specific" versus a single global 90 used throughout — one gives way. (b) "Two hundred years, wide range of institutions" versus 96 high-debt years clustered in a few countries and one era. (c) "We won't discriminate debt's genesis" versus "peacetime origins understate the effect" — you can't set a factor aside and also use it.
- **Change list leaves out.** Currency composition, maturity, the reverse direction, and any third factor (a banking crisis) that raises debt and cuts growth together. Barro's tax-distortion route predicts the same thing by a different path; nothing here separates them.

**5. Where the parts came from.** The dataset is **built** — worked out and criticised. The buckets and both cutoff lines are **fitted** (tuned on the data, no outside grip). The mechanism is **asserted**.

**6. What would make it harder to vary.** Two jobs would tighten it most: (1) fix the cutoffs and the weighting *before* looking, then show the kink survives re-weighting and dropping the dominant countries — otherwise 90 stays loose. (2) A poke that separates direction, e.g. debt inherited from wars, or spreads that move before the line is crossed.

**7. What this does not show.** Passing is not truth, and failing is not falsehood. The 90 may be loose while some association is real; the data contribution stands on its own.

**8. One next step.** Write the prediction down first, then re-run the exercise weighted by country size with each country left out in turn.
